segments.text: Watch parallel rays pass through two curved glass surfaces and crowd toward a common focus.
Now zoom in. The outer rays cross before the central rays, so one point cannot catch them all.
How can we predict this mismatch without pretending a real lens is infinitely thin?
Trace each ray: find the next surface, change its direction, then repeat.
A ray marks a local direction of light travel. It is not the complete electric field.
Store a starting position and a unit direction vector. Distance along that direction is our variable.
In uniform material, a ray follows a straight line. A boundary can change its direction.
Our lens has two spherical surfaces, four millimetres apart, with glass index one point five.
You see a central slice of a three-dimensional calculation. The optical axis runs horizontally, along z.
Curvature, thickness, and aperture specify the glass. We still need to calculate where light goes.
First, extend the incoming line until it meets the first spherical surface. Calculate that intersection.
Substitute the ray into the sphere equation. A quadratic gives two possible roots, one, or none.
But our optical surface is only a spherical cap. A root on the opposite cap must be rejected.
Keep a forward intersection on the correct cap, inside the clear aperture. Otherwise, report a missed surface.
At the accepted point, construct the normal. For a sphere, it follows the line through its centre.
Orient the normal into the next medium. Measure bending from this local direction, not from the optical axis.
Split the incoming unit direction into parts tangent and normal to the interface.
The phase variation along that interface must match on both sides. That determines the tangential part.
Divide the first refractive index by the second. Multiply the tangential direction by this ratio.
From air into glass, the ratio is below one. The ray bends toward the normal.
Rebuild the normal component to make a unit vector. Choose the branch entering the next medium.
This is vector Snell refraction. The familiar sine law describes the same rule using angles.
From glass into air, the tangential part grows. Beyond the critical angle, no real transmitted direction exists.
That is total internal reflection. Our transmitted path stops; following the reflected branch requires another trace.
Find the second surface using the new direction. A thick lens requires two separate refractions.
Recompute the normal and exchange the refractive indices. This time, the ray leaves glass for air.
Intersect the outgoing line with a detector plane. This point is the ray's predicted landing position.
Repeat across the entrance aperture. Every path shown comes from surface intersections and Snell refraction.
Near the axis, ray angles are small. Linearizing their motion gives the paraxial focus, marked here.
That focus is a useful reference, not a promise for every ray through a finite lens.
Open the aperture without changing the lens. Outer rays now sample steeper surface regions.
Watch the enlarged focus. For this spherical lens, outer rays cross the axis before central rays.
This mismatch is spherical aberration. It comes from the geometry, not a coarse numerical grid.
Move the detector. The bundle narrows and spreads, but its rays never all meet.
Here, best focus minimizes the root mean square distance from the spot centroid. Other criteria can differ.
Tilt the input. The off-axis pattern changes, so an on-axis test cannot describe the whole image.
Closing the aperture reduces geometric spread but rejects light. A smaller ray spot is not the whole story.
These are geometric paths. Their landing points are not a diffraction point spread function.
Waves still spread through a finite aperture, as in episode three. Closing the aperture can increase diffraction blur.
Our ideal surfaces use one fixed index. We omit reflected power, dispersion, absorption, and manufacturing errors.
A missed surface or total internal reflection is a tracing outcome. Check those before comparing image errors.
Other surface shapes use the same logic. More rays sample the chosen model more densely; they do not add missing physics.
One ray follows one recipe: intersect, construct the normal, refract, and continue.
A bundle reveals the consequences. Aperture, field angle, and detector position all affect the geometric image.
The paraxial focus starts the design. Exact surface tracing tests the finite lens within its assumptions.
Next, we will choose lens shapes using image error, while keeping the required focal length.
